raw_case_text: A 73-year-old male came to our hospital due to worsening dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain for 1 month. He had received chemotherapy (vincristine, melphalan, lenalidomide, pomalidomide) and steroid therapy over 10 months for multiple myeloma until 2 weeks before. An initial chest X-ray reported ill-defined opacities in both lungs. A non-contrast high-resolution CT revealed a mosaic pattern of multifocal ground-glass opacities in both upper and mid lungs (Fig. 1A). In addition to it, there were also noted multiple subpleural nodules (size 1-3 cm in diameter) in both lower lungs (Fig. 1B, C). These nodular lesions had an irregularly marginated but well-defined border. At this time, the initial clinical suspicion was an atypical pneumonia. Laboratory testing revealed leukocytopenia. The patient received a 10 day-course of antibiotics (imipenem/cilastatin and levofloxacin), which did not result in any significant clinical improvement. Follow-up contrast-enhanced chest CT taken in 10 days after the initial CT scan showed disappearance of multifocal ground-glass opacities (Fig. 1D) but persistent existence of multiple subpleural nodules without any change in size and extent. These nodules showed homogenous low attenuation showing an average of 40 Hounsfield unit (HU) on post-contrast CT with 20 HU net contrast enhancement (Fig. 1E). There was no significantly enlarged mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Percutaneous CT-guided transthoracic needle biopsy was done and the core biopsy specimen showed well-formed necrotic granulomas containing Pneumocystis jiroveci micro-organisms (Fig. 1F). No other organisms were found. The patient was initiated on trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) therapy for 3 weeks. After 10 days since the patient started on TMP-SMX therapy, follow-up chest radiographs showed gradual decrease in extent of nodules in both lungs with improvement of symptoms. The last follow-up chest radiograph obtained 16 days later showed near-complete disappearance of nodules, and he was uneventfully discharged in stable condition.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 73-year-old male with multiple myeloma presented with a 1-month history of worsening dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain two weeks after completing 10 months of multi-agent chemotherapy and corticosteroid therapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had been treated over the preceding 10 months (until 2 weeks prior to presentation) with vincristine, melphalan, lenalidomide, pomalidomide, and corticosteroids for multiple myeloma. He presented to the hospital with a 1-month history of progressively worsening shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain.
subjective.past_medical_history: Multiple myeloma treated for 10 months with vincristine, melphalan, lenalidomide, pomalidomide, and corticosteroids.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for worsening dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain for 1 month.

objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory test: Leukocytopenia. Initial chest radiograph: Ill-defined bilateral lung opacities.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial non-contrast high-resolution chest CT (HRCT): Mosaic pattern of multifocal ground-glass opacities in both upper and mid-lungs, accompanied by multiple well-defined, irregularly marginated subpleural nodules (1–3 cm in diameter) in both lower lungs. Day 10 follow-up contrast-enhanced chest CT (after 10 days of imipenem/cilastatin and levofloxacin): Complete disappearance of the upper/mid-lung ground-glass opacities, but unchanged persistence of the bilateral lower lobe subpleural nodules (showing homogeneous low attenuation of ~40 HU with 20 HU net contrast enhancement and no mediastinal lymphadenopathy). CT-guided percutaneous transthoracic core needle biopsy of a subpleural nodule: Demonstrated well-formed necrotizing granulomas containing Pneumocystis jirovecii microorganisms with no other pathogens identified.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Nodular granulomatous Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (presenting as multiple 1–3 cm bilateral lower lobe subpleural necrotizing granulomatous nodules alongside transient upper/mid-zone ground-glass opacities) in a multiple myeloma patient following 10 months of chemotherapy and corticosteroids, definitively confirmed by CT-guided percutaneous transthoracic core needle biopsy. Plan and clinical course: After failing a 10-day empiric course of imipenem/cilastatin and levofloxacin, the patient was treated with a 3-week course of oral/IV trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX). Follow-up chest radiographs at 10 and 26 days after starting TMP-SMX demonstrated near-complete resolution of the bilateral pulmonary nodules and symptoms, and he was discharged in stable condition.
